result.markdown: # Tutorial 1: Simple regression, diagnostics, and model usefulness {#i-ep01 .unnumbered} ::: {.outcomes} By the end of Tutorial 1, you can - fit a simple regression in R and interpret its results with units, - check the assumptions of a model with residual plots and influence measures, - judge a model with its coefficient table, $R^2$, and the F-test, - check an AI reading of a regression output and correct its errors. ::: Tutorials are exam preparation sessions. The tasks below are exam-style questions. You take the exam in TestVision, and R is available. Try each task yourself before you look at the solution. You may use AI for this, following Attempt, Ask, Verify, Explain. ::: {.course-phase .phase-before} ## Before class Complete the after-class practice from Lectures 1 and 2. Lecture 3 is on the day before this tutorial: read its lecture material, and do its practice after the tutorial. Keep the sections for Lectures 1 to 3 of the [QM Intermediate Code Sheet](code-sheet.qmd) open while you work. If the notation slows you down, review [Mathematics Refresher: straight lines, slopes, and intercepts](../resources/math-refresher.qmd#straight-lines-slopes-and-intercepts) and [powers, roots, and squared deviations](../resources/math-refresher.qmd#powers-roots-and-squared-deviations). Write from memory: 1. the simple linear regression model, 2. the fitted line, 3. the residual, 4. the formula for $R^2$, 5. the null hypothesis of the overall F-test. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your preparation 1. $Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\varepsilon_i$. 2. $\widehat Y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1X_i$. 3. $e_i=Y_i-\widehat Y_i$. 4. $R^2=1-\text{SSE}/\text{SST}=\text{SSR}/\text{SST}$. 5. $H_0:\beta_1=0$ in simple regression (all slopes zero in general). ::: ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-in-class} ## In the tutorial A complete written answer does five things. It names the sample, shows the calculation, and reports values with units. It interprets the values in context. And it states one important limit of the model or of the data. More practice for home is in the final section of this page, [Extra practice for home](#i-ep01-home). All six tasks follow one founder question through the steps of Lectures 1 to 3: when founders offer more equity, how much equity do they end up giving in the deal? Before a pitch, every founder decides which share of the company to offer. On Shark Tank the sharks often accept the amount of money but ask for a larger share in return. A founder who knows how the final share is related to the opening offer can choose the offer with the likely final share in mind, and can decide in advance how far to go in the negotiation. All tasks use the Shark Tank teaching file. The code below loads the data and keeps the 882 pitches that ended in a deal on air (`deals`). Two variables answer the question, both in percent of the company: the equity that the founder offered at the start of the pitch (`equity_offered_pct`) and the equity that the founder gave in the deal (`deal_equity_pct`). A difference between two shares is measured in percentage points. Review [percent and percentage points](../resources/math-refresher.qmd#numbers-proportions-percentages-and-units) if you need to. In eight of the deals the sharks invested without taking a share of the company, so the file records a deal share of 0%. These deals stay in the sample, because 0% is the equity that these founders gave. The last line prints the number of pitches and the number of deals. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) deals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1) # pitches with a deal on air c(pitches = nrow(sharks), deals = nrow(deals)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` pitches deals 1441 882 ``` ::: ::: ### Task 1: Fit and interpret (Lecture 1) [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Fit the simple regression of the equity given in the deal (`deal_equity_pct`) on the equity offered by the founder (`equity_offered_pct`), with all deals. Then report: 1. the sample, with its number of deals, 2. the fitted equation, 3. the interpretation of the slope with units, in one sentence, 4. the size of the slope for an offer that is one standard deviation higher, in percentage points, as a percent of the mean deal share, and in standard deviations of the deal share, followed by one sentence that judges the size, 5. the limit of the intercept's meaning, in one sentence. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text R code: Sample: Fitted equation: Interpretation of the slope: Size of the slope for one standard deviation more equity offered: Limit of the intercept's meaning: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer The code fits the model and prints its two coefficients. It then prints the mean and the standard deviation of the deal share, the benchmarks for the size of the slope, the standard deviation of the offer, and the smallest and largest offer. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} equity_model <- lm(deal_equity_pct ~ equity_offered_pct, data = deals) coef(equity_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) equity_offered_pct 8.315024 1.207341 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(mean_deal = mean(deals$deal_equity_pct), # benchmarks, in % sd_deal = sd(deals$deal_equity_pct), sd_offer = sd(deals$equity_offered_pct)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean_deal sd_deal sd_offer 23.345329 14.878996 7.674459 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} range(deals$equity_offered_pct) # smallest and largest offer ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 51 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - R code: see the code above. - Sample: all 882 pitches in the file that ended in a deal on air. - Fitted equation: $\widehat y = 8.32 + 1.207x$, with the equity given in the deal $y$ and the equity offered $x$, both in percent of the company. - Interpretation of the slope: among the 882 deals, an offer that is one percentage point higher is associated with an equity given in the deal that is on average about 1.21 percentage points higher. - Size of the slope for one standard deviation more equity offered: the offers have a standard deviation of 7.67 percentage points, so $1.207\times7.67\approx9.27$ percentage points more equity given. This is about 40% of the mean deal share of 23.3% and $9.27/14.88\approx0.62$ standard deviations of the deal share. This is a large difference in the share of the company that a founder gives up. - Limit of the intercept's meaning: the intercept of 8.3% is the fitted deal share for an offer of 0%, and no founder offered less than 1%, so it has no useful business meaning of its own. ::: ### Task 2: Diagnostics and how the data were generated (Lecture 2) [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Produce the residual-versus-fitted plot and the normal Q-Q plot for the Task 1 model of the equity given in the deal on the equity offered. 1. Name two problems with the assumptions that you can see in the plots. For each one, say in one sentence what in the plots shows it. 2. Count the standardised residuals beyond $\pm 3$ and the observations with a Cook's distance above $4/n$. Say in one sentence what most deals with a standardised residual above 3 have in common. 3. The residual plot shows vertical stripes, and inside the stripes the points lie in rows. Count the offers and the deal shares that are a multiple of 5%. Then explain in two sentences how the way the data were generated produces this bunching, and why it is not a violation of an assumption. 4. Name one assumption that these plots cannot assess, and say in one sentence what information would assess it. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text R code: First problem, and what in the plots shows it: Second problem, and what in the plots shows it: Number with a standardised residual beyond ±3: Number with a Cook's distance above 4/n: What most deals with a standardised residual above 3 have in common: Offers and deal shares at a multiple of 5%: How the data were generated, and why the bunching is not a violation: Assumption the plots cannot assess, and what would assess it: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer The code draws the two plots side by side. It then prints - the standard deviation of the residuals in five groups of offers, - the two counts of flagged deals, - the number of flagged deals in which the sharks took the whole company, - the number of offers and deal shares at a multiple of 5%. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} equity_model <- lm(deal_equity_pct ~ equity_offered_pct, data = deals) old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE) par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.4, 1.3, 0.7), las = 1) plot(fitted(equity_model), residuals(equity_model), pch = 16, col = grDevices::adjustcolor("#0072B2", alpha.f = 0.35), bty = "n", xlab = "Fitted deal share (%)", ylab = "Residual (percentage points)") abline(h = 0, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#D55E00") qqnorm(rstandard(equity_model), pch = 16, col = grDevices::adjustcolor("#009E73", alpha.f = 0.40), bty = "n", main = "", xlab = "Normal theoretical quantile", ylab = "Standardised residual") qqline(rstandard(equity_model), col = "#D55E00", lwd = 2) par(old_par) offer_group <- cut(deals$equity_offered_pct, c(0, 4.99, 5, 10, 20, 100), labels = c("below 5", "exactly 5", "5 to 10", "10 to 20", "above 20")) round(tapply(residuals(equity_model), offer_group, sd), 1) # spread per group ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` below 5 exactly 5 5 to 10 10 to 20 above 20 3.1 10.6 11.0 11.3 18.0 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} rs <- rstandard(equity_model) c(big_rstandard = sum(abs(rs) > 3), above_3 = sum(rs > 3), above_3_whole_company = sum(rs > 3 & deals$deal_equity_pct == 100), cooks_flagged = sum(cooks.distance(equity_model) > 4 / nobs(equity_model))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` big_rstandard above_3 above_3_whole_company 15 14 8 cooks_flagged 34 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(offer_multiple_of_5 = sum(deals$equity_offered_pct %% 5 == 0), deal_multiple_of_5 = sum(deals$deal_equity_pct %% 5 == 0)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` offer_multiple_of_5 deal_multiple_of_5 745 686 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Residuals against fitted deal shares (left) and normal Q-Q plot of the standardised residuals (right), for the 882 deals.](t01-exam-prep_files/figure-html/fig-iep01-task3-1.png){#fig-iep01-task3 fig-alt='Two panels. Left: residuals against fitted deal shares between about 9 and 70 percent. The points form vertical stripes at round offers, narrow at the smallest fitted values and wider to the right, with a few residuals between 50 and 86 percentage points. Right: normal Q-Q plot whose points follow the line in the middle and bend sharply upwards at the right end, up to a standardised residual of about 7.' width=672} ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - R code: see the code above. - First problem, and what in the plots shows it: the residuals lie in a narrow band at the smallest fitted values and spread out more at larger fitted values. Their standard deviation grows from about 3 percentage points for offers below 5% to about 11 for offers of 5% to 20% and 18 for offers above 20%. This widening band shows heteroskedasticity, so it challenges homoskedasticity. - Second problem, and what in the plots shows it: the Q-Q plot leaves the line at the right end, with standardised residuals up to about 7.4. Some deals lie far above the line, so the right tail is much heavier than a normal tail, which challenges normality. - Number with a standardised residual beyond ±3: 15 deals, about 1.7% of the 882. - Number with a Cook's distance above 4/n: 34 deals, about 3.9% of the 882. - What most deals with a standardised residual above 3 have in common: in 14 of the 15 the founder gave far more than the fitted share, and in 8 of them the sharks bought the whole company (a deal share of 100%). - Offers and deal shares at a multiple of 5%: 745 offers (84%) and 686 deal shares (78%) are a multiple of 5%. Another 49 deal shares are about one third of the company, recorded as 33% or 33.3%. - How the data were generated, and why the bunching is not a violation: founders and sharks name these shares on the spot during a televised negotiation, so they choose round numbers such as 10%, 20%, 25%, a third, or a half. A share calculated with a valuation method would not bunch at these values. The bunching only shows that the offers and the deal shares take few distinct values, and it does not by itself challenge linearity, homoskedasticity, or normality. - Assumption the plots cannot assess, and what would assess it: the plots cannot assess independence. To assess it, you need knowledge of how the data were collected, for example whether deals in the same episode were negotiated by the same sharks on the same day. You may also notice that the 42 deals with an offer below 5% lie mostly below the line. Their average residual is about $-5.6$ percentage points, so the straight line overstates the deal share for the smallest offers. ::: ### Task 3: Coefficient inference (Lecture 3) [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Use the coefficient table and the 95% confidence intervals of the Task 1 model of the equity given in the deal on the equity offered. 1. Test $H_0:\beta_1=0$ against $H_1:\beta_1\ne0$ in five steps, with the critical value approach at the 5% level. 2. Calculate the 95% confidence interval for $\beta_1$ by hand from the estimate and the standard error, and compare it with the interval in the output. Then interpret the interval in one sentence, with units. 3. A slope of exactly 1 would mean that each extra percentage point offered adds exactly one percentage point to the deal share, so that the sharks take the same extra share on top of every offer. Say whether 1 lies inside the interval. Then test $H_0:\beta_1=1$ against $H_1:\beta_1\ne1$ at the 5% level, with $t=(\hat\beta_1-1)/\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_1)$, and state the conclusion in business terms in one sentence. 4. Would heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors fix both problems with the assumptions that you named in Task 2? Answer yes or no, and explain in one or two sentences. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text R code: Test, hypotheses: Test, test statistic: Test, critical value and rejection region: Test, observed value: Test, conclusion: Interval, formula: Interval, given values: Interval, calculations: Interval, lower and upper bound: Interval, comparison with the output: Interval interpretation: Slope of 1, inside the interval or not: Slope of 1, observed test statistic: Slope of 1, conclusion in business terms: Robust standard errors, yes or no, and why: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer The code prints the coefficient table, the 95% confidence intervals, the critical value, and the t statistic for a slope of 1. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} equity_model <- lm(deal_equity_pct ~ equity_offered_pct, data = deals) coef_table <- summary(equity_model)$coefficients coef_table ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 8.315024 0.7477311 11.12034 5.684681e-27 equity_offered_pct 1.207341 0.0511365 23.61017 7.368475e-96 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} confint(equity_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5 % 97.5 % (Intercept) 6.847480 9.782569 equity_offered_pct 1.106978 1.307705 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} qt(0.975, df = 882 - 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1.962663 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} (coef_table["equity_offered_pct", "Estimate"] - 1) / coef_table["equity_offered_pct", "Std. Error"] # t statistic for a slope of 1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4.054665 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - R code: see the code above. - Test, hypotheses: $H_0:\beta_1=0$, $H_1:\beta_1\ne0$. The significance level is 5%. - Test, test statistic: $T=\hat\beta_1/\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_1)$, with $882-2=880$ degrees of freedom. - Test, critical value and rejection region: $t_{0.975,\,880}$ = `qt(0.975, 880)` = 1.963. Reject $H_0$ if $|t_{obs}|\ge1.963$. - Test, observed value: the slope is $1.207$ with standard error $0.0511$, so $t_{obs} \approx 23.6$. - Test, conclusion: since $23.6\ge1.963$, reject a zero slope at the 5% level. Founders who offered a larger share gave a larger share in the deal, on average. The p-value, far below 0.001, gives the same decision. - Interval, formula: $\hat\beta_1\pm t_{0.975,\,880}\,\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_1)$. - Interval, given values: $\hat\beta_1=1.2073$, $\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=0.05114$, $t_{0.975,\,880}=1.963$. One more digit than usual avoids rounding error. - Interval, calculations: $1.2073 \pm 1.963 \times 0.05114 = 1.2073 \pm 0.1004$. - Interval, lower and upper bound: $(1.107,\; 1.308)$, in percentage points given per percentage point offered. - Interval, comparison with the output: the interval by hand matches the interval in the output. - Interval interpretation: under the model assumptions, the data are consistent with a population slope between about 1.11 and 1.31 percentage points of equity given per extra percentage point offered. For an offer one standard deviation (7.67 points) higher, this is about 8.5 to 10.0 points more equity given, a narrow range of large values. - Slope of 1, inside the interval or not: 1 lies below the lower bound of 1.107, so it is outside the interval. - Slope of 1, observed test statistic: $t_{obs}=(1.2073-1)/0.05114\approx4.05$. Since $4.05\ge1.963$, reject $H_0:\beta_1=1$ at the 5% level, the same decision as the interval gives. - Slope of 1, conclusion in business terms: founders who offered more gave more than one extra point per point offered, so the extra share that the sharks take on top of the offer grows with the offer, from about $8.32+0.207\times10\approx10.4$ points at an offer of 10% to about 12.5 points at an offer of 20%. - Robust standard errors, yes or no, and why: no. Robust standard errors address the heteroskedasticity only. They do not change the estimated line and do not address the heavy right tail of the residuals. With 882 deals the non-normality matters little for the tests, but the deals far above the line can still move the fit, which Task 5 checks. ::: ### Task 4: R² and F (Lecture 3) [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Use the Task 1 model of the equity given in the deal on the equity offered. 1. Calculate SST, SSE, SSR, and $R^2$ from the observed and the fitted values. 2. Compare your $R^2$ with the R-squared in the regression output. 3. Show that the overall F statistic equals $t^2$, with $t$ the t statistic of the slope. Name the two models that the overall F-test compares. 4. Write one concluding sentence that does not claim more than the data show. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text R code: SST, SSE, and SSR: R-squared by hand: R-squared in the output: F and t squared: The two models that the overall F-test compares: Concluding sentence: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer The code computes the three sums of squares from the observed and the fitted values, and then prints $R^2$ by hand, $R^2$ from the output, the overall F statistic, and the squared t statistic of the slope. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} equity_model <- lm(deal_equity_pct ~ equity_offered_pct, data = deals) y <- deals$deal_equity_pct yhat <- fitted(equity_model) SST <- sum((y - mean(y))^2) SSE <- sum((y - yhat)^2) SSR <- sum((yhat - mean(y))^2) c(SST = SST, SSE = SSE, SSR = SSR) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` SST SSE SSR 195039.77 119403.23 75636.54 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(R2_manual = 1 - SSE / SST, R2_summary = summary(equity_model)$r.squared, F_summary = unname(summary(equity_model)$fstatistic["value"]), t_squared = summary(equity_model)$coefficients["equity_offered_pct", "t value"]^2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` R2_manual R2_summary F_summary t_squared 0.3878006 0.3878006 557.4401201 557.4401201 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - R code: see the code above. - SST, SSE, and SSR: in squared percentage points, $\text{SST}\approx195{,}040$, $\text{SSE}\approx119{,}403$, and $\text{SSR}\approx75{,}637$, so $\text{SST}=\text{SSR}+\text{SSE}$. - R-squared by hand: $R^2=1-119{,}403/195{,}040\approx0.388$. - R-squared in the output: 0.388, the same value. - F and t squared: the overall F statistic is about 557.4. The t statistic of the slope is about 23.61, and $23.61^2\approx557.4$, as it must be in simple regression. - The two models that the overall F-test compares: the complete model and the intercept-only model, which predicts the mean deal share of 23.3% for every deal. - Concluding sentence: among these 882 deals, the equity offered explains about 39% of the variation in the equity given, so the offer is a useful guide to the typical deal share, but single deals often lie far from the line. ::: ### Task 5: Do a few deals drive the answer? (Lecture 2) [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Task 2 flagged 34 deals with a Cook's distance above $4/n$. Before a founder relies on the Task 1 line, check how much these deals move it. Fit the Task 1 model again without the flagged deals. The rule, a Cook's distance above $4/n$, is fixed before you look at the result. 1. Report the slope and the intercept of both fits, and the change of the slope in percent. 2. Calculate the fitted deal share for an offer of 10% in both fits. 3. State the three-step rule for handling a flagged observation, and say in one sentence which fit you would report as the main result. 4. Advise a founder who plans to offer 10% in two sentences. Use the residual standard error of the Task 1 model to say how far single deals lie from the fitted share. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text R code: Slope and intercept, all deals: Slope and intercept, without the flagged deals: Change of the slope: Fitted deal share for an offer of 10%, both fits: Rule for flagged observations, and the fit to report: Advice in two sentences: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer The code marks the flagged deals and fits the model without them. It then prints - the coefficients of both fits, - the change of the slope in percent, - the fitted deal shares for an offer of 10%, - the residual standard error of the model with all deals. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} equity_model <- lm(deal_equity_pct ~ equity_offered_pct, data = deals) flagged <- cooks.distance(equity_model) > 4 / nobs(equity_model) equity_model_kept <- lm(deal_equity_pct ~ equity_offered_pct, data = deals[!flagged, ]) rbind(all_deals = coef(equity_model), without_flagged = coef(equity_model_kept)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) equity_offered_pct all_deals 8.315024 1.207341 without_flagged 7.720026 1.193338 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 100 * (coef(equity_model_kept)[2] / coef(equity_model)[2] - 1) # change in % ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` equity_offered_pct -1.159826 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} new_offer <- data.frame(equity_offered_pct = 10) c(all_deals = unname(predict(equity_model, newdata = new_offer)), without_flagged = unname(predict(equity_model_kept, newdata = new_offer))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` all_deals without_flagged 20.38844 19.65341 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sigma(equity_model) # residual standard error, in percentage points ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 11.64841 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - R code: see the code above. - Slope and intercept, all deals: slope 1.207, intercept 8.32, with 882 deals. - Slope and intercept, without the flagged deals: slope 1.193, intercept 7.72, with 848 deals. - Change of the slope: about $-1.2\%$, a very small change. - Fitted deal share for an offer of 10%, both fits: about 20.4% with all deals and about 19.7% without the flagged deals, a difference of less than one percentage point. - Rule for flagged observations, and the fit to report: investigate, report, never silently delete. The flagged deals are real deals, such as the sharks buying the whole company, and the answer hardly changes without them, so the fit with all deals is the main result and the check without them is reported next to it. - Advice in two sentences: "For an offer of 10%, expect to give about 20% of the company in the deal, and decide before the pitch how large a share you are willing to give. Single deals typically lie about 11.6 percentage points above or below the fitted share, more than half of the fitted 20%, so be prepared for a final share well above or below this number." ::: ### Task 6: Check the AI (Lectures 1 to 3) [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Tom prepares a pitch. He gave the output of the Task 1 model of the equity given in the deal on the equity offered to an AI assistant. Here is the output: ```text Outcome: equity given in the deal (%), 882 deals Estimate Std. Error p-value Equity offered (%) 1.207 0.051 <0.001 Intercept 8.315 0.748 <0.001 R-squared: 0.388 ``` He asked: "How good is this model?" The AI answered: > "Good model. The equity offered predicts the deal share correctly for > about 39% of the deals, because $R^2$ is 0.388. A founder who offers one > percentage point more of the company gives, on average, about 1.2 > percentage points more in the deal. And the p-value of the slope is below > 0.001, which proves that the assumptions of the model hold." 1. The AI answer contains exactly two errors. Name each error and explain it in one sentence. 2. Write one correct sentence about the $R^2$ of 0.388. 3. State in one sentence what the small p-value of the slope does show. Then name in one sentence one result from Task 2 that Tom should know before he trusts this p-value. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text First error: Second error: Correct sentence about the R-squared: What the small p-value does show: A result from Task 2 to know before trusting the p-value: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer The code prints the share of the 882 deals whose residual is at most one percentage point away from zero, that is, whose deal share lies within one percentage point of the fitted value. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} equity_model <- lm(deal_equity_pct ~ equity_offered_pct, data = deals) mean(abs(residuals(equity_model)) <= 1) # share within 1 point of the fitted value ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.1564626 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - First error: $R^2$ is the share of the variation in the deal shares that the fitted values explain, not a share of deals that the model predicts correctly, and only about 16% of the deals lie within one percentage point of their fitted value. - Second error: a p-value is calculated under the assumptions of the model, so it cannot prove that they hold. - Correct sentence about the R-squared: "Among these 882 deals, the equity offered explains about 39% of the variation in the equity given in the deal." - What the small p-value does show: it is strong evidence against a slope of zero, if the assumptions of the model hold. - A result from Task 2 to know before trusting the p-value: the spread of the residuals grows with the offer, so the homoskedasticity assumption fails and the usual standard error and p-value may be wrong. The second sentence of the AI answer is correct as a description of the 882 deals. It matches the interpretation of the slope in Task 1. ::: ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-after} ## After class ### Individual practice [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Do the sharks pay the amount that a founder asks for? Use all 882 deals (`deals`). Regress the amount agreed in the deal on the amount that the founder asked for, both in thousands of dollars. The code below keeps the deals and converts both amounts from dollars to thousands of dollars. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} deals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1) deals$ask_1k <- deals$ask_amount_usd / 1000 # amount asked, in $1,000s deals$deal_1k <- deals$deal_amount_usd / 1000 # amount agreed, in $1,000s ``` ::: 1. The fitted equation is $\widehat{\text{agreed}}=27.6+1.009\,\text{asked}$, both in \$1,000s. The Q-Q plot rises steeply at the right end, so the residuals are far from normal. The usual standard errors are therefore only a rough guide. Say in one sentence whether an offer of 10% lies inside the range of offers in the data, and why this matters for the prediction. 2. The founder ends up giving 30% of the company. Calculate the residual of this deal, and give it as a percent of the fitted value. 3. Interpret the sign of the residual in one sentence. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text R code: Fitted deal share: Inside the range of the data, and why it matters: Residual: Meaning of the sign: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer The code prints the fitted deal share for an offer of 10% and the residual of a deal at 30%, both in percent of the company. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} equity_model <- lm(deal_equity_pct ~ equity_offered_pct, data = deals) fitted_10 <- unname(predict(equity_model, newdata = data.frame(equity_offered_pct = 10))) c(fitted = fitted_10, residual = 30 - fitted_10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` fitted residual 20.388438 9.611562 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - R code: see the code above. - Fitted deal share: with $x=10$, $\widehat y = 8.315 + 1.2073 \times 10 \approx 20.4$, so about 20% of the company, twice the offer. - Inside the range of the data, and why it matters: the offers in the data run from 1% to 51%, and 309 deals started with an offer of exactly 10%, so the prediction rests on many similar deals and does not extrapolate. - Residual: $e = 30 - 20.4 = 9.6$ percentage points, about 47% of the fitted value. - Meaning of the sign: the positive sign means that this founder gave more equity than the fitted mean deal share of founders who offered 10%. ::: #### Task 8: Significant, but is it large? Interpret the slope with units, in one sentence, and state whether it is significantly different from zero at the 5% level. 2. Judge the size of the slope in three ways: as a percent of the mean amount agreed, in standard deviations of the amount agreed, and at the lower and the upper end of its 95% confidence interval. 3. Report $R^2$, and explain in one or two sentences why a slope can be significant while $R^2$ is close to zero. 4. Write one sentence for a founder that reports both the significance and the size of the association. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text R code: Interpretation of the slope, and significance: Size as a percent of the mean amount agreed: Size in standard deviations of the amount agreed: Size at both ends of the 95% interval: R-squared, and why it can be small for a significant slope: Sentence for a founder: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer The code fits the model, prints the coefficient table, the 95% intervals, and $R^2$, and then the mean and the standard deviation of the amount agreed, the two benchmarks for the size of the slope. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks_model <- lm(deal_1k ~ number_sharks_in_deal, data = deals) summary(sharks_model)$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 231.33410 27.50160 8.411659 1.621022e-16 number_sharks_in_deal 45.70094 18.95847 2.410582 1.613122e-02 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} confint(sharks_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5 % 97.5 % (Intercept) 177.357705 285.31049 number_sharks_in_deal 8.491843 82.91004 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} summary(sharks_model)$r.squared ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.006559982 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(mean = mean(deals$deal_1k), sd = sd(deals$deal_1k)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean sd 291.5433 342.7692 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - R code: see the code above. - Interpretation of the slope, and significance: a deal with one more shark is associated with an amount agreed that is on average about \$45,700 higher. With $t\approx2.41$ and p $\approx$ 0.016, the slope is significantly different from zero at the 5% level. - Size as a percent of the mean amount agreed: \$45,700 is about 16% of the mean amount agreed of about \$291,500. - Size in standard deviations of the amount agreed: $45.7/342.8\approx0.13$ standard deviations, a small difference compared with how much deal amounts vary. - Size at both ends of the 95% interval: the interval runs from about \$8,500 to \$82,900, which is about 3% to 28% of the mean amount agreed. The data are consistent with a very small and with a sizeable association. - R-squared, and why it can be small for a significant slope: $R^2$ is about 0.007, so the number of sharks explains less than 1% of the variation in the amounts agreed. With 882 deals the average difference is estimated well enough to be significant, but single deal amounts vary so much that the number of sharks says little about any one deal. - Sentence for a founder: "Deals with one more shark are associated with an amount agreed that is on average about \$46,000 higher, about 16% of the mean deal, but this estimate is uncertain and the amount of a single deal depends much more on other things than on the number of sharks." ::: #### Task 9: A regression line from summary statistics (Lecture 1) A start-up sells online courses. Over 30 weeks it recorded its weekly advertising spend $X$, in hundreds of euros, and the number of new sign-ups $Y$. The summary statistics are: | | Mean | Standard deviation | |:---|---:|---:| | Advertising spend $X$ (€100s) | 12 | 4 | | New sign-ups $Y$ | 85 | 20 | The correlation between $X$ and $Y$ is 0.6. 1. Calculate the slope and the intercept of the fitted line, and write the fitted equation. 2. Interpret the slope with units, in one sentence. Then say in one sentence what it implies for the advertising cost per extra sign-up. 3. Calculate the fitted number of sign-ups for a week with €1,500 of advertising. 4. Judge the size of the slope: by how much do the fitted sign-ups differ between two weeks whose advertising spend differs by one standard deviation? Give the answer in sign-ups, in standard deviations of $Y$, and as a percent of the mean of $Y$. 5. Calculate $R^2$ and interpret it in one sentence. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text Slope, formula and calculation: Intercept, formula and calculation: Fitted equation: Interpretation of the slope: Advertising cost per extra sign-up: Fitted sign-ups at €1,500: Size for one standard deviation more advertising: R-squared and its interpretation: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer Filled-in structure: - Slope, formula and calculation: $\hat\beta_1=r\,s_Y/s_X=0.6\times20/4=3$ sign-ups per €100. - Intercept, formula and calculation: $\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x=85-3\times12=49$ sign-ups. - Fitted equation: $\widehat y=49+3x$, with $x$ in €100s. - Interpretation of the slope: a week with €100 more advertising is associated with on average 3 more new sign-ups. - Advertising cost per extra sign-up: €100 for 3 sign-ups, about €33 per extra sign-up, which the start-up can compare with the revenue of one sign-up. - Fitted sign-ups at €1,500: $x=15$, so $\widehat y=49+3\times15=94$ sign-ups. - Size for one standard deviation more advertising: $3\times4=12$ more sign-ups, which is $12/20=0.6$ standard deviations of $Y$ and about 14% of the mean of 85 sign-ups. In simple regression, one standard deviation more in $X$ always goes with $r$ standard deviations more in the fitted $Y$. - R-squared and its interpretation: $R^2=r^2=0.6^2=0.36$, so advertising spend explains 36% of the variation in weekly sign-ups in these 30 weeks. A check in R of the hand calculations: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} b1 <- 0.6 * 20 / 4 b0 <- 85 - b1 * 12 c(slope = b1, intercept = b0, fitted_at_15 = b0 + b1 * 15, one_sd_effect = b1 * 4, in_sd_of_y = b1 * 4 / 20, percent_of_mean = 100 * b1 * 4 / 85, r_squared = 0.6^2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` slope intercept fitted_at_15 one_sd_effect in_sd_of_y 3.00000 49.00000 94.00000 12.00000 0.60000 percent_of_mean r_squared 14.11765 0.36000 ``` ::: ::: ::: #### Task 10: A result without stars that is still informative (Lecture 3) A webshop with 250 product pages wants to know whether more product photos go with a higher conversion rate, the percent of visitors of a page who buy the product. The mean conversion rate is 3.2%. A simple regression of the conversion rate (in %) on the number of photos on the page gives this output: ```text Outcome: conversion rate (%), 250 product pages Estimate Std. Error p-value Number of photos 0.010 0.015 0.51 Intercept 3.150 0.090 <0.001 ``` The critical value for a 95% confidence interval is $t_{0.975,\,248}=1.970$. A professional photographer would add five photos to every page. 1. Calculate the 95% confidence interval for the slope, and say whether the slope is significantly different from zero at the 5% level. 2. Use the upper end of the interval to state the largest association with five more photos that the data are consistent with, in percentage points and as a percent of the mean conversion rate. Review [percent and percentage points](../resources/math-refresher.qmd#numbers-proportions-percentages-and-units) if you need to. 3. A colleague says: "No stars, so the result tells us nothing." Correct this statement in one or two sentences. Use (copy and paste) this structure: ```text Interval, formula: Interval, calculations: Interval, lower and upper bound: Significance at the 5% level: Largest association with five more photos: Correction of the colleague's statement: ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer The code repeats the hand calculations. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ci_photos <- 0.010 + c(-1, 1) * 1.970 * 0.015 ci_photos # interval for one more photo, in percentage points ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.01955 0.03955 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 5 * ci_photos[2] # upper end for five more photos ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.19775 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 100 * 5 * ci_photos[2] / 3.2 # as a percent of the mean conversion rate ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6.179688 ``` ::: ::: Filled-in structure: - Interval, formula: $\hat\beta_1\pm t_{0.975,\,248}\,\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_1)$. - Interval, calculations: $0.010\pm1.970\times0.015=0.010\pm0.0296$. - Interval, lower and upper bound: $(-0.020,\;0.040)$ percentage points of conversion per extra photo. - Significance at the 5% level: zero lies inside the interval, so the slope is not significantly different from zero (p $\approx$ 0.51). - Largest association with five more photos: $5\times0.040=0.20$ percentage points, a rise from 3.2% to at most about 3.4%, which is about 6% of the mean conversion rate. - Correction of the colleague's statement: the interval is narrow, so the result rules out large associations. Pages with five more photos convert at most about 0.2 percentage points better on average, and the webshop can compare this with the cost of the photographer. ::: [Continue to Lecture 4: Multiple regression and what controls do](i04-multiple-regression.qmd). :::
